Reviewer Consensus

Positive:

- AutoOpt-11k is seen as a valuable, much-needed dataset and benchmark at the intersection of CV, NLP, and optimization.
- The framework is a compelling proof-of-concept that tailored pipelines can outperform generalist LLMs.
- Release of resources makes it impactful for the community.

Negative:

- Reviewers want clearer focus on dataset contribution rather than mixing too many elements.
- Lack of metadata, systematic evaluation, and error analyses raises concerns about robustness and reproducibility.
- Practical motivation and design choices (multi-stage vs direct approaches) need stronger justification.

Reviewers appreciate AutoOpt-11k as a timely and well-executed dataset contribution, with impressive pipeline results. However, they caution that the paper is overextended, under-analyzes key design choices, and leaves open questions about dataset reliability, practical use cases, and pipeline design.

author_final_remarks.value:
Dear Reviewers, Area Chairs, and Program Chairs,

This study has two major contributions:

1) AutoOpt11k: Image dataset of 11000 handwritten and printed mathematical optimization models, representing real-life problems in engineering, business, and science domains.

2) AutoOpt: A unified framework that uses AutoOpt11k dataset for training the modules of framework. A user only needs to provide an image of optimization program and the problem gets solved automatically without any human inference.

The following computational experiments were performed in response to reviewer comments:

•	Statistics on inter‐annotator agreement between 5 annotators are reported with explanation of experimental setup.

•	Ablation studies are performed and the results are reported.

•	Performance of framework is measured using:

1. Framework-level evaluation: efficiency of entire pipeline (M1-M2-M3) is measured: 94.20%, and

2. Module-level evaluation : efficiency of entire pipeline is evaluated based on the performance of individual module M1 (89.83%), M2 (91.75%), and M3 (100%), which yields (0.8983 x 0.9175 x 1) x 100 = 82.41% (Lower bound).

•	Performed an experiment where 500 test problems were solved using AutoOpt and ChatGPT-4o. For 432 instances, AutoOpt was better compared to ChatGPT and for 68 instances, the results obtained from both approaches were the same. Most of the time ChatGPT failed to generate even feasible solutions with message like: “*it seems I can’t do such advanced analysis right now*”.

•	Convergence plots and variance bars over multiple runs are obtained.

•	The relevant studies suggested by reviewers (OptiMUS, LLaMoCo, EoH) are referred and compared with our study and included in study.

•	Usefulness of each stage in practical scenario, to ensure correct conversion from image, to perform sensitivity analysis by modifying objective function and constraint co-efficients, to modify pipeline by joining other optimization solving mechanism at backend, to train students and professionals in operation research, is explained.

We are thankful to all reviewers for their comments as we sincerely believe that their suggestions helped us to improve the quality of study.

The updated study, through its contributions, touches multiple domains:

1. *Artificial Intelligence* (Optimization Problems Dataset and AutoOpt framework),

2. *Image Processing* (Mathematical Expression Recognition),

3. *Operations Research* (Bilevel optimization based decomposition method).

Comment 1: 

Response: We will definitely include the discussions and references in the paper. Thank you for your feedback as this will allow us to position our work clearly in comparison to other papers.


Comment 2: 

Response:  We agree with your suggestion. We will revise the introduction and other relevant parts of the paper to position our work and the contributions very clearly.

Comment 3: 1. & 2.

Response: Since both 1. and 2. are related questions, we answer it together.

As per our design choices at the beginning of the study, we decided to create a large dataset for “Image to LaTeX” and a subset for “Image/LaTeX to Pyomo”. The Image/LaTeX to Pyomo dataset is only 10% of the original “Image to LaTeX” dataset. We perceived mathematical image to text as a more difficult task as compared to text to text at the start of the study, and therefore chose the dataset sizes accordingly.

To answer your question, we did not perform picture-to-pyomo experiments while working on the initial manuscript. After we received your comment, we did try picture-to-pyomo experiments, however, given the small size of the image-pyomo dataset, the experiment results were not favorable. We believe that any such experiment that leads to good performance on picture-to-pyomo will require a much larger image-pyomo dataset.

We agree with you that Pyomo is indeed a machine-friendly modeling language. Below we provide our thought process without arguing that Image-to-Latex is better than Image-to-Pyomo in terms of machine friendliness or data utility. We chose LaTeX as an intermediate representation as we thought that it provides a symbolic and easily interpretable format that closely mirrors how optimization problems are written. If a mistake is made in the image-to-LaTeX stage, one can fix that in isolation, rather than having to debug the Pyomo code which is more verbose as compared to LaTeX. This was completely motivated by our design choices and we agree that we could have taken that approach that you are suggesting.


Comment 3:
3.
 
Response: You are absolutely correct on this. Almost every optimization toolbox is compatible with python-based scripts and as you already mentioned, one can go from Image-to-Pyomo (i.e. Python code) directly. Our current dataset facilitates that learning, however, image-to-pyomo is a subset of image-to-latex, which leads to limited training samples. If you give us an opportunity, we can resolve this by increasing the size of image-to-pyomo subset and provide the results of the image-to-pyomo model in the paper. We would also like to highlight that both OptiMUS and LlaMoCo also use LaTeX in some form at the intermediate steps.


Comment 3:
4.
 
Response : Very often in the classroom when a business or engineering problem is discussed, the instructor as well as the students work out the mathematical formulation on the whiteboard, tablet or a paper in the form of an image. After this, the task of converting the problem into a programming language and solving it with a suitable solver, still remains. In most of the engineering and business schools there are quite a few sessions devoted on how to solve such problems after the mathematical model is ready. At times the students are not savvy enough to write LaTeX/Python code and rely on Excel Add-ins and other softwares (which still require encoding) to solve the problem. Incorporating the mathematical model is cumbersome and error-prone, and we believe that we are contributing here.

Consider this toy example: Assume that I have a small production unit where I am producing two products X and Y with profit contribution 7 and 8 dollars respectively. Both products consume two resources R1 and R2 in following manner; X:  R1|R2= 3|4 and Y: R1|R2= 6|3. R1 and R2 are available in limited quantities, i.e. 80 and 40 units, respectively. And I want to decide how many units of each product I should produce to maximize my profit. In literature, it is referred to as the product-mix problem. This problem when discussed in the classroom is formulated as follows:

Maximize 7x+8y 

3x+6y≤80 (R1 constraint)

4x+3y≤40 (R2 constraint)

x≥0,y≥0

Our method will facilitate solving this problem as soon as the model is ready. Interestingly, some of the papers that you have highlighted attempt to convert the description of the problem to a mathematical model as written above, while we contribute on the task that follows after that. Optimization experts who work as operations managers, consultants, process engineers or supply chain managers, also formulate such optimization problems which are often very large and much more complex and cannot be easily converted into a mathematical model from its description. However, once the mathematical model is available, our approach will be useful to solve such industry grade problems. Our dataset has small to large scale optimization problems and will benefit the optimization community in simplifying the solution step.

For Comment 1, I like the authors for disclosing a discussion on related works. The three relevant works should be added into references, as well as the discussion you provided.

For Comment 3, thanks for the authors to interpret their design choices. Following questions still need to be addressed:

1) have you conducted experiments on picture-pyomo? I can not see why Latex is a machine-friendly format. while pyomo code not.

2) explain why "decomposing the problem as image->LaTeX and LaTeX->Pyomo" allows improved data utility.

3) I am curious if we could just translate the picture into python-written objective function like OptiMus and LLamoco, since almost every optimization toolbox can be compatible with python coded objective functions.

4) the authors have not directly answered my initial question: can you list a scenario where we have to take a photo of optimization problems and them solve it? Provide an example will definitely convince me this work is truly useful.

Response: We agree that we have not provided metadata on variable/constraint counts/sparsity patterns. Additionally, certain constraints may also be set constraints so it is not possible to give the count (like Ax <= b, and size of matrix A (i.e., number of rows and columns) is not known). Dear reviewer, we sincerely thank you for your constructive comments. Below, we provide a detailed explanation of how each comment has been addressed.

Comment 1: A more systematic review on automating algorithm design or code generation is needed. I suggest three papers: OptiMUS, LLaMoCo, and EoH.

Response 1: We have reviewed each of the suggested studies and we found them useful. However, there is a significant difference between the current and suggested studies as follows:

1) OptiMUS: This study primarily focuses on the development of LLM based agents to consider optimization problem available in words (i.e., Abstract form) and generate mathematical formulation by interpreting the decision variables, objective function, constraints, and parameters. Later, the programmer (or AI agent) is expected to type the code and solve the problem using a commercial Gurobi solver that can handle only linear or quadratic problems. Interestingly, our contribution starts where OptiMUS ends. Once a mathematical model is ready, we convert the model into a computer code and then use a solver that can adaptively solve all kinds of optimization problems by interpreting the structure of the problem within the computer code.

2) LLaMoCo: This study (similar to OptiMUS) also focuses on obtaining a mathematical formulation from the abstract form of a given optimization problem.

Both Study 1 and Study 2 (OptiMUS and LLaMoCo) only lead to the mathematical model creation, it clearly shows that we are addressing the gap on how one can automatically solve an optimization problem once the mathematical model is available.

3) EoH: This study is a review on how certain heuristics can be designed using LLMs to solve certain classes of optimization problems and is therefore different from our work. We will cite this paper and highlight how our work significantly differs from this study.
 
Overall, based on the literature review, we observed that most studies are primarily focusing on the use of LLM to obtain the mathematical formulation of the optimization problem given in abstract form, whereas our study begins with this output (mathematical formulation) and focuses on the automation of the entire problem solving procedure. Our proposed dataset and pipeline would in fact support the automation of Study 1 and Study 2 that have shown limitations for very large scale problems. 

Comment 2: Overall, the authors put too many content into this paper, which makes the real contribution of this paper unclear to the readers. Can you refine the content and strengthen the contribution on your proposed dataset?

Response 2: We are sincerely sorry if the presentation of the paper made the core contribution unclear. We will surely revise the content as per your suggestions. In the meantime, we would like to highlight the key contributions of our study for your kind consideration:

As the paper is submitted in the dataset and benchmark track, the core focus of the study is on proposing the AutoOpt-11k dataset. In this dataset, the optimization formulation is present in image form along with its labels, i.e., LaTeX and Pyomo code. Every example in the dataset has been labeled by experts with substantial effort with the complete LaTeX formulation and the Pyomo code needed to solve the formulation. We utilized this dataset in our framework (Modules M1, M2 and M3) to show how it enables the automation of optimization problem solving. We will try our best to clarify our contributions and reorganize the paper. Additionally, the proposed dataset is highly heterogeneous (Table 1, Table 2 and Appendix 1) and would be able to automate optimization problem solving for problems that appear in business, engineering, and science domains.

Comment 3: I am wondering if the usage case described in this paper is truly important to realistic engineering scenario. In particular, why we have to take a photo of the optimization problems? If a person has capability of writing formula of optimization problems, should not he is capable of writing the latex or computer program of that optimization? Besides, why we have to translate the picture of an optimization problem to latex first and then translate the latex to PYOMO? Why not directly train a model to translate picture to PYOMO or other programming modelling language? From my angle, this could be more convenient.

Response 3: As per the standard procedure of solving optimization problems described in literature, the first step is to develop a mathematical model by identifying the basic components such as decision variables, objective function, and constraints (Winston, 2004). Once this mathematical model is created, next steps require coding the model on the computer and then using an appropriate solver to solve it. Thus, the steps of formulating and solving an optimization problem are as follows:

Step 1: Mathematical model creation (often written in mathematical language on paper or whiteboards or tablets) based on     business or engineering objectives and constraints

Step 2: Encoding the model in a programming language

Step 3: Identifying an appropriate optimization algorithm (solver) to solve the coded model

We automate Step 2 and Step 3 through our unified framework. Through our contributions solvers (commercial and opensource) would no longer be restricted to typed inputs but can now interpret real-world images, handwritten formulations, or textbook snapshots.

Once Step 1 is done, the next steps can be quite cumbersome as the mathematical model may contain hundreds or thousands of decision variables and constraints. In mathematical syntax, models are often written in concise notation, but translating it into computer code and solving it requires effort. To the best of our knowledge, there are no studies that do this and the current LLMs are highly error prone if used for Step 2 and Step 3. The dataset proposed by us will be useful to train multimodal LLMs that can understand the optimization formulations in images and solve it by identifying the structure of the problem using a solver. We are confident that the proposed dataset will be of significant value to the entire optimization community.

Regarding your question on why we have to translate the picture of an optimization problem to LaTeX first and then translate the LaTeX to PYOMO, we address this as follows: 

You are absolutely correct in pointing this out as to why we do not jump from image to code directly. We can surely do that and our current dataset facilitates that training. In fact we considered solving the problem with the approach that you have suggested, but chose to take a two step approach for the following reasons. 

1) In literature, mathematical formulations are mainly available in PDF or Image format or handwritten format. These formats are human friendly but not machine friendly, i.e., the data available in images cannot be easily interpreted by the machines directly. LaTeX is one such format that can be easily interpreted by the machine or algorithm. One can use this LaTeX output for different uses/experiments apart from generating the Pyomo script like our study. Further, we also wanted to first convert this data into a LaTeX format so as to allow the user to visualize the optimization problem in machine-encoded text format. 

2) In case a complex optimization problem image is converted directly to a code, it would be difficult for the user to identify if any errors have crept in. Converting the image to LaTeX will allow the user to check if the computer has read the image properly. Once the image is in the form of LaTeX, converting it into a code so that it can be solved by a solver is a mechanical text-to-text conversion problem and it is easy to train deep learning models that can handle such tasks very efficiently.

3) Once the model is available in LaTeX, one can do certain intermediate tasks as well, like updating the model, such as adding additional variables or constraints, performing sensitivity analysis, etc. It will be slightly hard to do in a Pyomo code as it is more structured and comparatively easier if done in the LaTeX format. Once the model is in LaTeX, one can also target other modeling backends instead of Pyomo, like AMPL, Lingo, etc.

4) Finally, decomposing the problem as image->LaTeX and LaTeX->Pyomo allows each module to be trained, improved and reused independently which enhances the utility of our dataset as well as the modules. We still agree with you that one may go from image->Pyomo directly, and it will have its own set of benefits.

Reference: Winston, Wayne L. Operations research: applications and algorithms. Thomson Learning, Inc., 2004.

summary.value: This paper presents AutoOpt-11k, a dataset of 11,000 images of handwritten and printed mathematical optimization models spanning single‐objective, multi‐objective, bi‐level, and stochastic formulations. It also introduces a three‐stage pipeline: (1) a tailored MER (Mathematical Expression Recognition) model to convert images into LaTeX, (2) a fine‐tuned LLM to translate LaTeX into executable Pyomo code, and (3) a bilevel‐decomposition solver (BOBD) to solve the generated models. The authors report state‐of‐the‐art BLEU scores for MER versus leading LLMs and superior solver performance on benchmark problems. The dataset, code, and trained models are publicly released.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. AutoOpt-11k fills a gap by offering a dedicated dataset for image‐to‐code research in mathematical optimization.
2. The unified vision→NLP→solver framework promotes cross‐community research and serves as a valuable baseline for future work.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Lack of metadata on variable/constraint counts, sparsity patterns, or domain provenance limits understanding of dataset heterogeneity.
2. No inter‐annotator agreement statistics or error‐checking protocols are reported; mislabeled LaTeX or code could skew both MER and text‐to‐code evaluations.
3. The process by which target optimizations were generated (parameter choices, human selection vs. automatic pipelines) is not described in sufficient detail, raising questions about annotation consistency.
4. Key design decisions—choice of network backbone for MER, BOBD hyperparameters, LLM fine‐tuning dataset—are not systematically ablated.
5. It is unclear how sensitive M3 is to errors in M1/M2—no end-to-end ablation quantifies error propagation through the pipeline.

summary.value: This paper propose a dataset where the input is  handwritten or printed optimization problems, and the label is the latex or modelling language representation of the given problems. The dataset is created by hunman-experts and through strict human-in-loop correction and validation. With such high-quality dataset, the authors propose a exploratory study on how to end-to-end solve optimization problems in pictures through a three-stages approach. This approach proposed by the authors first trains a image-to-text model (CNN + Transformer) to extract latex representation from the handwritten or printed optimization problems. Then it fine-tunes a small-scale coding LLMs to translate Latex of an optimization problem to a mathematical language PYOMO, which further facilitate automatic solving by using the proposed bi-level optimization strategy in stage 3. The experiments show that the data in the proposed dataset is of good quality to train small-sized non-LLM model that outperforms LLMs on image-to-text extraction. The authors also showcase how to automatically solve one examplified problem instance using their end-to-end workflow.

strengths_contributions.value: I think the most important contributions of this paper are in two-folds: a) the proposed dataset is very valuable to the optimization community, where the different writing styles and variations in typeset are shown. Such dataset is key to exploring how to automate optimziation problem solving in the future and should be appreciated. b) the experimental conclusion is valuable to exsiting LLM-assisted optimization works, which indicate that the data quality and demain-specific knowledge are more important than model selection to some extends. As shown in the paper, a small CNN+Transformer architecture is sufficient to attain better optimization problem identification ability than general multi-modal LLMs such as powerful GPT-4o.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. A more systematic review on automating algorithm deisign or code generation is needed. I suggest three papers: OptiMUS (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10172) and LLaMoCo (https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.01131) and EoH (https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02051). There are more.

2. Overall, the authors put too many content into this paper, which makes the real contribution of this paper unclear to the readers. Can you refine the content and strengthen the contribution on your proposed dataset?

3. I am wondering if the usage case described in this paper is truly important to realistic engineering scenario. In particular, why we have to take a photo of the optimization problems? If a persom has capability of writing formula of optimziation problems, should not he is capable of writing the latex or computer program of that optimization? Besides, why we have to traslate the picture of an optimziation problem to latex forst and then traslate the latex to PYOMO? Why not directly train a model to traslate picture to PYOMO or other programming modelling language? From my angle, this could be more convenient.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: I recommend accept this paper after 2-runs discussion with the authors. I think the dataset proposed is the most valuable contribution of this paper, and am convinced that the dataset is reasonble and backed up with realistic usage and meaning.

summary.value: This paper presents AutoOpt, a framework for automating optimization problem solving from image-based mathematical formulations. It introduces AutoOpt-11k, a dataset of 11,554 handwritten and printed optimization models with LaTeX and PYOMO labels, created by 25 experts and verified in two phases. The framework comprises three modules: M1 (Image_to_Text) converts images to LaTeX using a hybrid deep learning model, M2 (Text_to_Text) generates PYOMO scripts from LaTeX, and M3 (Optimization) solves problems via a Bilevel Optimization-based Decomposition (BOBD) method. Experiments show AutoOpt-M1 outperforms ChatGPT, Gemini, and Nougat on MER tasks, while BOBD yields better results on complex problems than traditional methods. The dataset and framework could advance research at the intersection of computer vision, NLP, and mathematical optimization.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The paper proposes a comprehensive benchmark that contains various types of optimization problems with image input. The dataset contains various types, including handwritten and typeset. This benchmark would be beneficial for the community to better explore the capability to solve optimization problems with images.
- The benchmark is designed in three stages to transform the image to LaTeX and finally to the PYOMO script. The annotations are made with great effort, including annotations by experts with double checks.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- Interestingly, the PDF of this article appears to be an image, making it impossible to jump to paper citations or add text annotations while reading. This seems to relate to the importance of understanding text in images.

- The framework separates the whole image into the solution process into 3 stages. However, the proposed method is only compared to current models, such as GPT and Gemini, in the M1 stage. Have you considered combining these three stages to test the ability of current models to solve these image optimization problems in an end-to-end manner including stages of M1~M3?

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: I went through the dataset link and code roughly and think it contains dataset  as stated in the paper.

additional_feedback.value: I think the dataset is comprehensive and beneficial for the community, and the major concern is that the model is not evaluated on the whole three stages, instead is only evaluated in M1 statge.

final_justification.value: Thanks for the rebuttal. As I think this dataset is beneficial to the optimization and (multi-modal) large language models, my main concern lies in the evaluation unifying M1~M3. Though in the original paper the three stages are separately evaluated, in the rebuttal the authors make additional experiments and provide a rough estimation for the unified evaluation. I hope the authors can make revisions accordingly in the paper to emphasize the unified evaluation, which would make this paper more complete. I raise my point to 4.

title.value: AutoOpt: A Dataset and a Unified Framework for Automating Optimization Problem Solving

abstract.value: This study presents AutoOpt-11k, a unique image dataset of over 11,000 handwritten and printed mathematical optimization models corresponding to single-objective, multi-objective, multi-level, and stochastic optimization problems exhibiting various types of complexities such as non-linearity, non-convexity, non-differentiability, discontinuity, and high-dimensionality. The labels consist of the LaTeX representation for all the images and modeling language representation for a subset of images. The dataset is created by 25 experts following ethical data creation guidelines and verified in two-phases to avoid errors. Further, we develop AutoOpt framework, a machine learning based automated approach for solving optimization problems, where the user just needs to provide an image of the formulation and AutoOpt solves it efficiently without any further human intervention. AutoOpt framework consists of three Modules: (i) M1 (Image_to_Text)- a deep learning model performs the Mathematical Expression Recognition (MER) task to generate the LaTeX code corresponding to the optimization formulation in image; (ii) M2 (Text_to_Text)- a small-scale fine-tuned LLM generates the PYOMO script (optimization modeling language) from LaTeX code; (iii) M3 (Optimization)- a Bilevel Optimization based Decomposition (BOBD) method solves the optimization formulation described in the PYOMO script. We use AutoOpt-11k dataset for training and testing of deep learning models employed in AutoOpt. The deep learning model for MER task (M1) outperforms ChatGPT, Gemini and Nougat on BLEU score metric. BOBD method (M3), which is a hybrid approach, yields better results on complex test problems compared to common approaches, like interior-point algorithm and genetic algorithm.
